Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 28,018.

This is one of the earliest, and best, of the upcoming generation of stadiums, and even if it is on the outskirts of Bolton, its bold design makes it a local landmark.

When it was the Macron Stadium, one of its several previous incarnations, I interviewed Tyson Fury there - and he threatened to have my jaw broken.

When it was the Macron Stadium, one of its several previous incarnations, I interviewed Tyson Fury in a room at the hotel that was part of the Toughsheet Community Stadium in the build-up to his world title fight with Wladimir Klitschko.

After he’d claimed the Klitschkos were part of a devil-worshipping ring, Fury made some rather unpleasant comments about his views on links between homosexuality and paedophilia.

When the interview was printed, he did not seem best pleased with the results. He said his brother, Major Shane, was going to break my jaw ‘completely’ with a straight right hand.

‘See big Shane there?’ Fury said. ‘Have a look at big Shane. He’s 6ft 6in and 25st. He’s going to break (your) jaw completely with one straight right hand. I ain’t going to do it, ‘cos I’ll get in trouble. But the big fella, there – he’ll annihilate (you), won’t he? So Oliver, take a good look at him, because that’s the face you’re going to see before you hit the deck.’.

Sources indicate that fun times. I’ve never found quite the same level of excitement in watching Bolton Wanderers there, although it had some great days in the 2000s when it was called the Reebok and Sam Allardyce was the manager.

It is one of the earliest, and best, of the new generation of stadiums, and even if it is on the outskirts of the town, its bold design makes it a local landmark.

Division: Championship Opened: 1899 Capacity: 20,899.

Fratton Park has not lost the intensity and the raucousness that makes it such a hostile place to visit for opposing teams.

Since Luton Town's brief sojourn in the Premier League, everyone has become aware of the entrances to their Kenilworth Road ground, through what appears to be the ground floor of a terraced house.

But the old way in to Fratton Park, beneath a half-timbered gable, is even more charming.

One of the old institutions of English football, the stadium has been renovated but has not lost the intensity and the raucousness that makes it such a hostile place to visit for opposing teams.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1884 Capacity: 29,813.

Portman Road is still a wonderful stadium, a ground at the centre of its community, where you can breathe in the legends of Sir Alf Ramsey and Sir Bobby Robson.

Industry observers note that the matchday hospitality of the Cobbolds, the former owners of Ipswich Town, was legendary amongst journalists. I missed out on those days but a visit to Portman Road is still a treat.

It is still a wonderful ground, a ground at the centre of its community, a ground where you can breathe in the legends of Sir Alf Ramsey and Sir Bobby Robson, great football men who did great things in their time in charge of the club.

A few years ago, I went to the launch of Kieron Dyer’s autobiography in a suite at the stadium and it was a night that underlined how important the club is to the town.

Recent findings suggest that it is a joy to see that the current hierarchy value the importance of the stadium and have lavished care and money on it. It is one of the great outposts of the English game.

33. Molineux, Wolverhampton Wanderers.

Division: Championship Opened: 1889 Capacity: 31,750.

Molineux is a stadium whose four stands are named after club legends and previous owner and benefactor Sir Jack Hayward, and which takes care to respect its glorious past.

When I first started going to Molineux, it was dominated by a peculiarity.

One of the stands, the John Ireland Stand as it was then, was about 100ft from the touchline, a matter of much mirth for visiting fans.

It has been renamed the Steve Bull Stand now and the pitch has been repositioned so that the modern Molineux is a stadium that makes sense.

It is an arena to be proud of again for Wolves fans, a stadium whose four stands are named after club legends and previous owner and benefactor Sir Jack Hayward, and which takes care to respect its glorious past.

Division: Championship Opened: 1883 Capacity: 21,990.

Turf Moor is a wonderful place to watch football, where you can gaze out over the town and its mills.

Turf Moor is a wonderful place to watch football.

Sit in the North Stand, opposite the Bob Lord Stand, and you can gaze out over the town and its mills, which do not look quite as dark and satanic any more, and remember that you are in the traditional northern heartlands of our game here.

I have a friend from Burnley who insists that more people per head wear the jersey of their hometown club in Burnley than in any other football centre in England.

This is a club, after all, that may be bouncing between the Premier League and Championship now but which won the league title in 1921 and 1960 and was once a giant of the game here.

Stoke seems to have been put on a pedestal for thier ability to provide a hostile environment for visiting teams – but Turf Moor can serve up the weather and the atmosphere to run it close.

In a recent development, 31. The Hawthorns, West Bromwich Albion.

Division: Championship Opened: 1900 Capacity: 26,688.

The Hawthorns is the highest league ground in England, sitting on its perch above the M5, and it is also one of football’s great theatres.

I have seen a few crackers at The Hawthorns.

The 5-5 draw between West Brom and Manchester United in May 2013 that was Sir Alex Ferguson’s last game as a manager is probably top of the list.

Industry observers note that I was in the press room there in May 2017 when Chelsea sealed the title under Antonio Conte and the players invaded his press conference to shower him in champagne and generally rough him up. Conte did not look best pleased.

The highest league ground in England, sitting on its perch above the M5, it is also one of football’s great theatres, a ground where the support exudes a love for the game and a warmth that survives the vicissitudes of the club’s fortunes on the pitch.

30. Cledara Abbey Stadium, Cambridge United.

Division: League One Opened: 1932 Capacity: 8,024.

Cambridge might be in League One but the noise inside the Abbey Stadium would have put plenty of Premier League grounds to shame.

I made it to the Abbey Stadium for the first time on New Year's Day 2025 for the game against Reading.

I walked to the ground down Cut Throat Lane and stood on the terraces at the Newmarket Road End where the singing is at its loudest and where the names and shirts of the celebrated early 1990s team of John Beck, which included Dion Dublin, are painted on the wall at the back of the stand.

Cambridge might be in League One but the noise inside would have put plenty of Premier League grounds to shame.

In a recent development, 29. Deepdale, Preston North End.

Division: Championship Opened: 1878 Capacity: 23,404.

In a recent development, I love going to Deepdale just for the history. Just to gaze down from the stands and know this is where Tom Finney once played is enough to make it a memorable experience.

And the sense of it being a pilgrimage is only enhanced by the fact that one of the best statues in football sits outside the ground.

Sources indicate that I love going to Deepdale just for the history of the place. Just to gaze down from the stands and know that this was where Tom Finney once played is enough to make it a memorable experience.

And the sense of it being a pilgrimage is only enhanced by the fact that one of the best statues in football sits outside the ground.

Taking its inspiration from the 1956 sports photo of the year, which showed Finney aquaplaning through a huge puddle at Stamford Bridge, the sculpture, known as The Splash, immortalises Finney outside his hometown club.

It’s a wonderful tribute outside an arena redolent with memories of one of England’s greatest players.

28. Kenilworth Road, Luton Town.

Division: League One Opened: 1905 Capacity: 10,265.

Luton will move to a new stadium at Power Court in the city centre in a few years but Kenilworth Road will be missed.

The stadium entrance goes straight through the middle of a row of terraced houses.

The first time I went to Kenilworth Road was 43 years ago. I stood on the open terrace that hosted the away fans for an FA Cup fourth round tie that Manchester United won 2-0.

The most recent time I went was in November 2021, to see Neil Warnock break the record for the most games managed in English football but unable to stop his Middlesbrough team falling to a 3-1 defeat.

According to recent reports, across those decades, the atmosphere at the old stadium has endured. The Main Stand, which is more than a hundred years old, shook that night as Luton took Boro down and the stadium became a bear pit.

In a recent development, it attained a kind of fame all over again when the club’s return to the top flight recently focused attention on the quirky Oak Road End entrance that goes straight through the middle of a row of terraced houses. Luton will move to a fresh stadium at Power Court in the city centre in a few years but Kenilworth Road will be missed.

Sources indicate that 27. Etihad Stadium, Manchester City.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2002 Capacity: 61,038.

The Etihad is this high on the list because it’s witnessed one of the best teams in English football history - even if that all feels a little tainted now.

I’d probably have Maine Road in the top three in this list if Manchester City still played there. I loved that ground. I loved the benches in the Platt Lane stand, I loved standing on the Kippax, I loved the cantilever Main Stand and the alleyways around the ground and walking across Platt Fields to the game.

Sources indicate that but the Etihad isn’t Maine Road. It’s this high on the list because it’s in Manchester and it’s witnessed one of the best teams in English football history playing on its turf, marshalled by one of the game’s great managers – even if all that feels a little tainted by City's guilty verdict in their case with the Premier League, subject to appeal.

City have done their best to breathe personality into it but it’s hard to disguise the fact it’s a characterless, identikit modern stadium.

The corporate denizens of the Tunnel Club, traipsing back to their seats well after the whistle has blown for the start of the second half, don’t help, either.

Recent findings suggest that 26. Rodney Parade, Newport County.

Division: League Two Opened: 1877 Capacity: 8,722.

Not far from the banks of the River Usk, it’s a modern stadium with remnants of character that come into its own when the giants come to play for the FA Cup.

A Cardiff taxi driver once told me that the best fights in Wales happen outside Newport railway station late on Saturday nights. He said he sometimes took a break just to go and watch the action.

Rodney Parade’s a fine place to watch sport, too. Not far from the banks of the River Usk, it’s a modern stadium with remnants of character that come into its own when the giants come to play in the FA Cup.

I was there a few years ago when Manchester City visited in the fifth round and after the game, the way out for fans took them past the open windows of the small changing rooms behind one of the goals where you could hear the celebrations of Pep Guardiola’s team booming out into the South Wales night.

Like the railway station, it’s not a place for the faint-hearted.

25. Nigel Eady County Ground, Swindon Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1892 Capacity: 15,547.

Industry observers note that my most recent trip to the County Ground was a 0-0 draw with Accrington Stanley last year. It wasn’t the best game but I had the best time.

Sources indicate that there were more than 20 years between my first visit to the County Ground and my most recent, a 0-0 draw with Accrington Stanley in March 2025. It wasn’t the best game but I had the best time.

I’d had a week of being abused on social media by Newcastle fans (which is part of the job and, yes, I agree, I don’t have to read it) and going to Swindon felt like a wonderful breeze blowing on my face.

Recent findings suggest that for a start, there were more than 7,000 supporters there, for a fourth-tier game which meant nothing to both teams in terms of promotion or relegation. The atmosphere was lively and passionate and the ground has character and warmth, even if one of the ends was closed.

According to recent reports, at half-time, I watched a DS Active match between lads with Down Syndrome representing Swindon and Bristol City and it was a joy. It was a joy to see their uncomplicated joy in the beauty of football and the way they celebrated their goals and their skill and the way they looked for their parents in the stands when they scored and the way they supported their team-mates.

The match was a reminder of what it means for a football club to be at the heart of its community. A stadium is about more than just a game.

Sources indicate that 24. American Express Stadium, Brighton & Hove Albion.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2011 Capacity: 31,876.

Maybe it is the knowledge of where Brighton & Hove Albion came from to get here that makes a visit to the Amex Stadium such an uplifting thing.

Maybe it is the knowledge of where Brighton & Hove Albion came from to get here that makes a visit to the Amex Stadium such an uplifting thing.

I remember seeing them at the Goldstone Ground, which I loved, but also at the Withdean Stadium, which is a glorified parks pitch inside a small athletics stadium.

When you have commuted to ‘home’ games at Gillingham’s Priestfield Stadium for two years as well, it is little wonder the Amex still feels like the promised land.

Neat on the inside, bold on the outside, it is a fitting home for an exceptionally well-run club and a fanbase that never gave up on its team.

23. Gtech Community Stadium, Brentford.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2020 Capacity: 17,250.

Brentford pulled off an architectural wonder with the Gtech, squeezing it into a parcel of land in the shadow of the raised section of the M4 in west London.

It is not often one of the new-build generation of English football stadiums has more character than a club’s former ground but the Gtech Community Stadium is a happy exception.

Griffin Park was much beloved, of course, and its peculiar feature of boasting a pub at each of the four corners of the ground was part of the game’s folklore. But Brentford pulled off an architectural wonder with the Gtech, squeezing it into a parcel of land in the shadow of the raised section of the M4 in west London.

The club has frequently had one of the best home records in the Premier League since coming up in 2021, which is testimony not just to the excellence of the players and manager but to the tight confines of the ground and the atmosphere it creates.

It has been revealed that it is no surprise it is attracting supporters who previously considered themselves without an affiliation. It is the type of stadium, and club, that makes fans feel they belong.

Division: Championship Opened: 1801 Capacity: 10,500.

I’m not one of those who regards the Ryan Reynolds/Rob McElhenney takeover of Wrexham with distaste.

I went to a lot of games in Wrexham in the late 70s and early 80s. My best mate, Bryn, was from the town so when his mum and dad took him to visit family there, I went along and we headed for the Racecourse Ground.

I’m not one of those who regards the Ryan Reynolds/Rob McElhenney takeover of the club with distaste, although I am aware that my friend and colleague Ian Herbert, a Wrexham fan and a club scholar, has had some misgivings.

Nothing in football is ever quite as wholesome as it seems but so far, it feels as if it has been good for the club and for the town.

According to recent reports, I don’t know what their long-term motives are but they have poured a lot of money into the team and into the infrastructure, and the club has risen and risen through the leagues. It’s bringing more light into a community that has had its share of hard times.

I was at the Racecourse, by the way, when Mark Hughes scored his spectacular overhead kick against Spain in 1985. It’s still one of the top five goals I’ve ever seen live.

(The others: Angel Di Maria for Argentina at the Lusail Stadium in the 2022 World Cup final, Zlatan Ibrahimovic for Sweden against England at the Friends Arena in 2012, Dennis Bergkamp for the Netherlands against Argentina at the Stade Velodrome at France '98 and Norman Whiteside for Manchester United against Everton at Wembley in the 1985 FA Cup final).

21. St Andrew's, Birmingham City.

Division: Championship Opened: 1906 Capacity: 29,409.

There are wealthy owners at Birmingham now, of course, and big intends, but St Andrew’s is still at the heart of everything.

Down the winding stairs from the press box, though the main reception area where staff are trying to sort ticket requests, through the foyer, down another set of steps and into a tunnel below the Main Stand where four garden forks hang on the wall outside the groundsman’s room – St Andrew’s is still a beautiful stadium that mixes old-school elements and modern stands.

According to recent reports, it’s a great place to watch a game. If it gets overshadowed by Aston Villa and West Brom, it still feels as if the soul of the Second City is alive in this place.

There are wealthy owners now, of course, and big plans, but St Andrew’s is still at the heart of everything.

Industry observers note that 20. Stadium of Light, Sunderland.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1997 Capacity: 48,095.

Sunderland have some of the best supporters in the country and the noise the fans make when the biggest occasions present themselves is up there with anyone.

Industry observers note that I’ve never been quite sure what to make of its successor, the Stadium of Light. I’m not even sure about the name, which is dramatic, certainly, but is also an obvious copy of the original Benfica ground in Lisbon – which opened in 1954 and held 130,000 at its peak.

The design is rather uninspiring for such an evocative name, too. It’s uncomfortably close to identikit upcoming-build, but I have friends who say it’s their favourite anywhere.

Industry observers note that the stadium does sit proudly atop the bluffs of the River Wear and it’s wonderful to see the team on the up again and back in the Premier League. 19. Bramall Lane, Sheffield United.

Division: Championship Opened: 1855 Capacity: 32,050.

Bramall Lane's Kop singing the Greasy Chip Butty song is one of the iconic experiences in English football.

Bramall Lane is still the only ground where I’ve sat in the dugout during a league game.

Neil Warnock is a friend of mine and when he was in charge at Sheffield United, he let me sit next to him in an end-of-season Championship game against Ipswich Town. I got a front row seat for Rob Kozluk, one of the game’s great sledgers, doing his best to wind up then-Ipswich boss Joe Royle.

I can’t think of many better grounds to have had the privilege. Bramall Lane is a cauldron of noise, full of history and passion, in the heart of the city.

Its Kop singing the Greasy Chip Butty song is one of the iconic experiences in English football.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1877 Capacity: 40,044.

All stadiums change and modernise with the years but there are few stadiums which have changed as dramatically as Stamford Bridge.

All stadiums change and modernise with the years but there are few stadiums which have changed as dramatically as Stamford Bridge.

It was once an intimidating place, dominated by the Shed, a sprawling, boisterous semi-circular terrace behind one of the goals that was synonymous with the crowd problems of the 1970s and early 80s.

It has been revealed that going to watch a Chelsea game now is an entirely different experience. The transformation began under Ken Bates, one of a group of visionary businessmen who changed the way we watch football, and then continued under Roman Abramovich.

And now, for many, going to Chelsea, with its towering West Stand and opulent corporate boxes, is a boutique experience not out of place with the hugely affluent area in which it stands.

It has been revealed that you can still feel the history of the place when you visit, though. To its credit, the club preserved the original wall that stood at the back of the Shed and it remains in place, used to display pictures of Chelsea legends.

Maybe I should declare a certain bias here, too: the food in the press room at the Bridge is the best in the Premier League.

According to recent reports, 17. Selhurst Park, Crystal Palace.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1924 Capacity: 25,194.

A trip to Crystal Palace's Selhurst Park is one of the best experiences in the English game.

I used to be put off by what I saw, pathetically, as the difficulty of getting to Selhurst Park in south London. Difficult to drive to, hard to find a parking space, not on the Tube, etc, etc.

I got over that some time ago. A trip to Palace is one of the best experiences in the English game.

The atmosphere generated by the Holmesdale Road stand, in particular, makes Selhurst Park one of the best grounds in England to watch football.

In a recent development, other clubs have seen the volume of their support dim as the demographic of their fans has changed but that has not happened at Selhurst Park. It is one of the few places left that has the power to intimidate and it is all the better for that.

According to recent reports, 16. MATRADE Loftus Road, Queens Park Rangers.

Division: Championship Opened: 1904 Capacity: 18,193.

One of the great surviving community grounds, a beautiful, steep-sided gem of a boutique stadium in Shepherd’s Bush, Loftus Road is a place to cherish.

One of the great surviving community grounds, a beautiful, steep-sided gem of a boutique stadium in Shepherd’s Bush, Loftus Road is a place to cherish.

When Bernie Ecclestone was a part-owner of the club, I sat in the directors’ box with him a few times and got shushed by Flavio Briatore for talking too much when my neighbour kept asking me questions. That may have been the first time anybody has ever been accused of talking more than Flavio.

The football wasn’t the best during their time there but the hospitality was: they had Mayfair restaurant Cipriani doing the catering.

They are long gone now but the stadium still remains, a wonderful anachronism in a changing world.

According to recent reports, 15. City Ground, Nottingham Forest.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1898 Capacity: 30,404.

Sometimes, just the walk to a stadium is part of what makes it special - take Nottingham Forest's City Ground for example.

Sometimes, just the walk to a stadium is part of what makes it special.

According to recent reports, my favourite was always the walk through Queens Gardens in Perth to the WACA. The stroll down from the city centre to the Adelaide Oval is beautiful, too, and the walk along the Thames to Craven Cottage is part of what makes that ground special.

Industry observers note that it’s the same with the City Ground. I always park in the same spot, near the River Trent, and walk along the river path until you can see the Forest fans streaming down towards the entrances at the Trent End.

When you get closer, you see the majesty of Trent Bridge next to the City Ground, too, and you feel you’re right at the heart of British sport.

There’s so much history at the City Ground, so much achievement, so much tradition and such a stunning location. It’s a wonderful place to watch a game.

Division: League One Opened: 1901 Capacity: 17,904.

Home Park in Plymouth is one of the best football experiences in the league.

My affection for Home Park was well entrenched even before I took my seat in the lovely Mayflower Grandstand and watched one of the greatest FA Cup shocks of recent years unfold there in February 2025 when the Pilgrims beat Liverpool.

That was a day to cherish everything about Home Park and the Green Army and the proud local identity enshrined there.

The Mayflower Grandstand, which was renovated recently, remains a beautiful piece of stadium architecture, the staff and stewards are uniformly friendly and welcoming, and the ground occupies a handsome spot in a park on a hill not too far from Plymouth Hoe.

It’s one of the best football experiences in England.

Industry observers note that 13. Prenton Park, Tranmere Rovers.

Division: League Two Opened: 1912 Capacity: 15,012.

Tranmere Rovers' Prenton Park became a beloved second home for me for a while.

Recent findings suggest that prenton Park became a beloved second home for me for a while. Like Stockport, they used to play their home games on a Friday night for a time and that offered a chance to go and watch them under the lights.

According to recent reports, I loved Prenton Park and its sense of community and its noble old stands from the start. When I started work as a trainee on the Daily Post and the Liverpool Echo in the early 90s, I got to cover Tranmere in the glory days under Johnny King when John Aldridge, who had returned from Real Sociedad, was scoring for fun.

Recent findings suggest that the atmosphere inside the ground on some of those nights on the Wirral was electric. When I was a news reporter at the Echo, I even had to go round to the house of Tranmere’s midfielder Kenny Irons in Norris Green to check out a story.

Recent findings suggest that kenny had been playing football in his front garden and kicked a ball over a hedge into next door’s garden. His neighbour was an old lady and she wouldn’t give Kenny his ball back. When I pitched up on his doorstep, he saw the funny side.

Recent findings suggest that 12. Wham Stadium, Accrington Stanley.

Division: League Two Opened: 1968 Capacity: 5,278.

The Wham Stadium has improved out of all recognition since Andy Holt became involved and any visit to it is a visit to the heart of the difference one man can make to a community.

For once, I can turn a blind eye to the renaming of the ground as the Wham Stadium.

That’s because I know how much love and commitment and time and money the Stanley owner, Andy Holt, has put into the resurrection of his local team since he cleared its debts in 2015 when it was on the brink of folding.

According to recent reports, andy doesn’t get much thanks for it and continues to fund the club to the tune of £250,000 a year, despite having claimed he would step down last year. When he does, he will bequeath a lasting legacy in this part of Lancashire.

The ground has improved out of all recognition since he became involved and any visit to it is a visit to the heart of the difference one man can make to a football club and a community. Visionaries like Andy are few and far between in football and the game will be poorer for his absence.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1897 Capacity: 43,205 (temporarily reduced to 36,887).

Villa Park remains one of the great arenas in the English game, a ground dripping with history.

Once one of the great architectural jewels of the English game, Villa Park lost the beauty of Archibald Leitch’s magnificent original Trinity Road Stand in 2000 when it was demolished.

Its loss was a sign of how shabbily we treat the idea of protecting our football heritage in this country.

Sources indicate that despite that, Villa Park remains one of the great arenas in the English game. I stood on the old Holte End in 1983 to see Villa, then European Cup holders, play the mighty Juventus. In October 2024 I was there again when Unai Emery’s side beat Bayern Munich, the team they conquered in the 1982 European Cup final, in their home return to the Champions League.

The atmosphere that night, with the Holte End in full voice, was a wonderful reminder of the great occasions of the past at a ground that feels like stadium aristocracy.

Recent findings suggest that 10. Old Trafford, Manchester United.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1910 Capacity: 74,244.

Old Trafford's iconic Holy Trinity statue stands guard on the forecourt outside the stadium.

Old Trafford is still a magnificent stadium, redolent of so many triumphs and memorable nights.

Industry observers note that yes, the roof leaks and, yes, Old Trafford could do with a bit of love and attention but there is a magic about this stadium that can never fade. (At least not until Sir Jim Ratcliffe knocks it down and builds the 100,000-seat tourist attraction that is his vision of the football of the future).

Much of that comes from the glories it has witnessed. Sit in the Stretford End and gaze down at a pitch where Duncan Edwards once strode across the turf, George Best danced through the mud and where Bobby Charlton and Denis Law and Bryan Robson and Roy Keane and Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney have played.

Sources indicate that it is still a magnificent stadium, redolent of so many triumphs. Outside, on the forecourt, the Holy Trinity statue, a tribute to Best, Charlton and Law, is a place of pilgrimage. As is the Munich Clock, a poignant reminder of the loss of so many of the Busby Babes in 1958.

I was standing on the terraces there when United beat Diego Maradona’s Barcelona 3-0 in the Cup Winners’ Cup in March 1984 and it was one of the best atmospheres I’ve ever felt at an English league ground.

It has been revealed that it’s a wonderful place, one of the stadiums that can lay claim to nurturing a chunk of the heart of the English game. They just need a team to be worthy of it again.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1897 Capacity: 37,645.

I love Leeds United's Elland Road. Even before I get into the ground, I love Elland Road.

The statue of Billy Bremner, which is usually festooned with scarves and surrounded by tributes to Leeds fans who have passed away, should be a starting point for any visit.

I love Elland Road. Even before I get into the ground, I love Elland Road.

The statue of Billy Bremner, which is usually festooned with scarves and surrounded by tributes to Leeds fans who have passed away, should be a starting point for any visit.

At the other end of the emotional spectrum, fish and chip shops are a decent component of a matchday experience and Graveley's, on Elland Road itself, which has a long queue snaking up to its door from two hours before kick-off, is one of the best football chippies in the country.

The stadium is a proper cathedral of our game, too. One-club cities sometimes generate that kind of passion and it’s evident at Elland Road. I like the fact the stands are named after Don Revie, Norman Hunter, Jack Charlton and John Charles, not an IT tech giant or an airline or a waste management service.

And I love the singing of Marching On Together, a club anthem that dates back more than 50 years, not one of the manufactured club songs you hear at some stadiums these days that mark a cosmetic attempt at authenticity.

It has been revealed that you feel the heat of English football at Elland Road, you feel the intensity of it and what it means. At a lot of massive clubs, that feeling has been lost. But it's alive here.

Sources indicate that 8. St James' Park, Newcastle United.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1892 Capacity: 52,719.

Lots of stadiums are referred to as cathedrals but St James’ Park is the one that fits the description best.

Newcastle are leaning towards building a new stadium adjacent to the current site and moving to that. Please don’t.

Lots of stadiums are referred to as cathedrals but St James’ Park is the one that fits the description best.

Every time I arrive in the city and see St James’ staring down from its vantage point above it, it sends shivers down my spine.

Its position is a symbol of its importance to the city. Inside, it generates one of the best atmospheres in the country, its fans are among the most loyal and the Gallowgate End is one of the most revered sections in our football history.

According to recent reports, newcastle are leaning towards building a new stadium adjacent to the current site and moving to that. Please don’t.

Sources indicate that 7. Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Tottenham Hotspur.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The January transfer window is just over a month away from opening, with EFL clubs already scouting new potential players ahead of the month-long chance to bolster their squads.

For clubs that have players that are starring in their leagues, they're going to face a fight to keep hold of them when it's all said and done, and then there are clubs at various points in the standings of any division that are going to look to strengthen their options.

And for high-flying Huddersfield Town in League One, they have a number of players who may be of interest to teams higher up in the footballing pyramid than they at the moment are - one player is certainly being looked at by Championship clubs.

Football League World has been exclusively informed that Terriers hot-shot Joe Taylor is a wanted man in the second tier ahead of the mid-season window.

Despite Dutch winger Derensili Sanches Fernandes taking most of the praise and plaudits for the West Yorkshire outfit since his summer arrival from Excelsior, Taylor has been quietly going about his business as part of their dangerous attacking unit, having forced his way back into contention at the Accu Stadium following his loan out to Wigan Athletic in 2025-26.

The 24-year-old was shipped out temporarily by previous manager Lee Grant to the Latics, where he found his spark again, scoring 11 goals in half a season for them before returning to Town in the summer under new head coach Martin Drury.

Alongside the aforementioned Sanches Fernandes in a supporting attacking role, where the pair play behind more of a focal point such as Ashley Fletcher or Bojan Radulovic more often than not, Taylor has found the back of the net 10 times in League One already in just 14 outings, proving to be one of League One's best once again.

And that goalscoring performance is not going unnoticed, with FLW exclusively being able to reveal that managerless Swansea City, as well as struggling Burnley are both weighing up a move for the Welsh centre-forward in January.

Taylor has only sparringly played at Championship level before for Luton Town before getting his move to Huddersfield, but there are clubs looking at trying to get the attacker a move up the pyramid.

Swansea of course lost head coach Vitor Matos to Strasbourg last week, but it will not stop them eyeing up targets ahead of January, and Taylor is on their radar, even with a strike-force of Adam Idah, Ross Stewart and Zan Vipotnik to choose from - the latter was the Championship's top scorer last season but has failed to fire in 2026-27, and theoretically could be cashed in on to open up the space for another upcoming forward.

Burnley meanwhile are in the Championship relegation zone and haven't won in Fabio Celestini's four matches in charge - they have centre-forward options like Jamie Vardy, Zeki Amdouni and Andreas Hountondji, but with a lack of goals coming from that particular trio, Taylor is being considered as a January option.

Whether Huddersfield would cash in on Taylor mid-season with their promotion aspirations remains to be seen, but given he's under contract until 2029, it'll likely take a significant amount of cash to prise him away from Drury's squad.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Queens Park Rangers goalscoring icon, Charlie Austin, has hit out at Millwall boss, Alex Neil, following the Scot's criticism towards Hoops winger, Paul Smyth, following Saturday's heated all-London affair at The Den.

Rangers continued their recently impressive form with a third victory in five matches by defeating the Lions 1-0 in SE16, courtesy of Nicolas Madsen's strike in the first minute of first-half stoppage time.

However, it is fair to say that the remainder of the contest wasn't without controversy, as the hosts were reduced to 10 men just 15 minutes into the contest after Zak Sturge's late challenge on the Northern Ireland international winger.

Although the statistics certainly showcased that Julien Stephan's side could have won the game by more if they finished their 31 attempts at Lukas Jensen's goal, much of Neil's post-match press conference centered around Smyth's involvement throughout.

The Saturday lunchtime victory saw Rangers end the Championship's 16th matchweek in seventh on 27 points, whilst Millwall sit 16th with nine fewer points.

Smyth, 29, is capable of featuring on either flank, and certainly caused plenty of complications for the Lions defence on Saturday in his 74-minute cameo, although Neil certainly had differing opinions.

“I spoke to Smyth about diving on the pitch in general. We had five players booked, and most of them came from him falling over," he stated.

According to recent reports, “The sending off – if he’s not offside, he’s not offside. If it’s a sending off, it’s a sending off. I’ve always been really straightforward with that sort of stuff. If it’s found that he’s guilty and he deserves to be sent off, I’m not going to argue that.

Neil was also booked for a verbal altercation with the Rs man, adding: “I told him to stop diving.

“I think what it was, it’s an element of frustration, but I’ve watched Paul Smyth for years. He’ll probably come up here and tell you he never dives, but I’d beg to differ.”.

Austin is a former teammate of Smyth's at Loftus Road, having returned to W12 back in 2020, scoring 15 goals in 59 appearances during his second spell, which lasted for two seasons.

The 37-year-old now offers regular opinions on Championship developments, and he defended the 26-time international when asked on his YouTube channel to give a verdict on Sturge's dismissal.

Sources indicate that "I'm going to say yes," he said. "Paul Smyth does well there. He gets his body in the way and knows what's coming.

"Alex Neil comes out and claims he was diving all around the pitch. Shut up mate.

"You'd like to have Paul Smyth in your team," Austin stated.

In a recent development, "Seriously. The threat he gives when 'we' have the ball, but when 'we' haven't, he presses and uses his pace well. He entices defenders to get close to him, which brings a foul and he anticipates the touch is coming.

"He was great for QPR at the weekend.

"But, for Alex Neil to come out and say that, I thought it was a stupid and naive comment.".

Austin knows exactly what it takes to achieve promotion to the Premier League, having done exactly that with the Hoops and West Bromwich Albion.

The former striker was certainly encouraged by Rangers' performance against their London rivals this weekend, especially the way in which they continued to impose themselves on the contest despite the hosts' desire to remain defensively solid.

Rangers and Millwall fans, do you agree with Alex Neil or Charlie Austin? Comment below!

Neil's comments, unsurprisingly, split opinion depending on which side of the fence those who watched the 90 minutes sat on, but that doesn't take away from the threat Smyth can possess, with the attacker already scoring and assisting three goals this campaign.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With three wins in their last four matches, Sheffield United have found some form heading in to the busy December period.

And one of Chris Wilder's stars of the campaign has been Sydie Peck, who remained at Bramall Lane despite transfer attention from elsewhere, is operating on another level.

Peck went through the entire 2024-25 Championship season without scoring, but after notching five goals last season, he's already matched that tally from midfield in 16 outings in 2026-27 - adding three assists to that tally too.

Peck - who joined United from Arsenal's youth setup in 2021 - rarely plays together with fellow midfield youngster Oliver Arblaster, who came through the Blades academy, but they started alongside each other in the engine room in the 4-0 rout of Watford this past weekend.

That pairing has been a source of contention for many United supporters in recent times - Peck's run in the first-team on a regular basis only really began when Arblaster was sidelined with a knee injury two seasons ago, and the latter was left sidelined more often than not when he was fit and ready to return last year.

They worked pretty well together against an abject Hornets side, but Wilder seemed to object to a question posed to him about whether or not they can work as a good pairing on a regular basis.

Wilder seemed utterly bemused, noting they've only played together six times in midfield, winning three and losing two, and he believes that fans are waiting for Peck and Arblaster to 'fail' as a partnership for whatever reason - you can watch the full rant below.

Arblaster's emergence in Sheffield United's relegated Premier League team in 2024, following a stint on loan at Port Vale, was a genuinely exciting moment - despite the drop back to the Championship, United had a player that was ready to start week in, week out in the Championship.

Sadly, his knee injury set him back a year, but it allowed Peck to emerge from the shadows and become the player he has now developed into - whilst still a raw talent, there's a reason why Premier League clubs have been circling in recent times from the likes of Newcastle United and Sunderland.

If Peck continues to seriously impress, then Sheffield United will have a significant decision to make in the January window should bids arrive at their door - selling Andre Brooks, Callum O'Hare and Gus Hamer for decent money in the summer though could mean the club are in a stronger financial position than many think.

Every player has a price though, and with January fast approaching, there's a chance that the Peck and Arblaster partnership may not have that much time to flourish.

  • "The hype will only continue to grow!"Max Dowman that is delightful!
  • At this rate, Arsenal supporters will be looking forward to Carabao Cup matches as eagerly as any Premier League or Champions League game, simply because it will be a chance to watch Dowman again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is an obligation on all of us, from supporters to pundits and journalists, to remain calm and measured about footballers as young as Max Dowman. But, my word, he does make it difficult. Arsenal’s 16-year-old sensation continues to sparkle whenever he steps on to the field, and he did so again with this superb display against Ipswich Town.

"The hype will only continue to grow!"Max Dowman that is delightful! 👏 pic.twitter.com/UfFY1VSyXn.

At this rate, Arsenal supporters will be looking forward to Carabao Cup matches as eagerly as any Premier League or Champions League game, simply because it will be a chance to watch Dowman again. The forward’s age and inexperience means he is still used sparingly in those high-priority competitions. The League Cup, by contrast, may prove to be his domain over the coming months.

Recent findings suggest that dowman’s double at Portman Road made him just the second 16-year-old to score two goals in a game for a Premier League side. The first was Wayne Rooney, for Everton against Wrexham in 2002.

The two goals underlined why there is so much excitement around Dowman. The first was a demonstration of his prodigious dribbling ability, as he weaved through Ipswich’s defence and buried his shot with the weaker right foot. The second demonstrated his composure: a slotted finish, rolled in with ease.

Max Dowman nets his second of the game! 😍 pic.twitter.com/XRZ9GqZx3x.

Recent findings suggest that as Mikel Arteta approaches the point of signing a new contract in north London, one wonders how much the idea of developing Dowman will excite him as he looks to the future. Which manager would not want to coach a player of such natural ability? Which manager would not want to see how good he could be? The same is true of Marli Salmon, the 17-year-old defender who also impressed on Tuesday night.

Sources indicate that “A joy to have him,” remarked Arteta of Dowman. “It’s remarkable. It’s something very natural for him. He can deliver those actions effortlessly, I would say. What we have to do is look after him. He is 16. You don’t see that in this league. In other leagues in Europe, that’s a totally different context.

Recent findings suggest that “Having two teenagers playing for Arsenal at this level is so fulfilling. Because I’ve been there and just to be able to contribute to somebody’s career and dream, to be able to experience a game like tonight, is phenomenal. And yeah, medium and long term, we know that if they continue to develop in the way that they are, we are going to have two tremendous footballers.”.

"He was brilliant, he made the difference - we need to look after him" 🌟Mikel Arteta states Arsenal need to "be really cautious" with 16-year-old Max Dowman after he scored twice in Arsenal's 4-2 win over Ipswich 🔴 pic.twitter.com/1msJAEkK8z.

Dowman’s two goals, along with strikes by Noni Madueke and Mikel Merino, secured a comfortable victory for Arsenal against Premier League opponents. Ipswich scored a goal of their own, through Anis Mehmeti, but never seemed likely to cause the visitors too much bother. A late strike from former Arsenal player Chuba Akpom was only a consolation. “We found a way to fight back into it,” noted Gary O’Neil. “Losing by two goals to them isn’t a dreadful effort.”.

Dowman is already developing a trademark goal, of sorts. His first strike for the club, against Everton last season, came after he left an opponent face-down on the turf at the Emirates Stadium. He inflicted the same pain here upon poor Cédric Kipré, who tried to tackle the teenager in the seventh minute but ended up with a mouthful of grass.

It was an image that encapsulated Arsenal’s dominance in the early exchanges, as was the sight of Madueke firing in the second. The chance came after Bruno Guimarães and Merino, majestic in midfield, had monstered Ipswich’s attempts to play out from the back. Merino was dominant throughout, winning tackles with steel and then spinning away opponents with style. “He’s unbelievable,” remarked Arteta.

Arsenal’s long-term relationship with the League Cup is not a particularly healthy one. For a club of their stature, it is a source of mild embarrassment that they have not won this competition since 1993. They came close last season, reaching the final at Wembley, but were defeated by Manchester City.

It has been revealed that given the depth of Arteta’s squad, Arsenal really should reach the final again. If this is a tournament for the B-team, at least in these early stages, then Arsenal probably have the best B-team in the country. They started this game without any of Bukayo Saka, Declan Rice, Martin Odegaard, and Kai Havertz but were still extraordinarily strong in midfield and attack.

The only pre-match concern was their defence, which has been weakened by a couple of early-season injuries. Arsenal started with Salmon at centre-back and the teenager was in direct combat with the physical, sharp-elbowed threat of Ipswich striker Zian Flemming. He stood up to the challenge with determination and class.

Ipswich had made 10 changes following their victory at Crystal Palace at the weekend, which was an indication of where the Carabao Cup sits in their priorities. They were able to get into Arsenal’s penalty area but never gave the impression they could really hurt the Premier League champions, apart from when Mehmeti converted Jack Clarke’s low cross.

In a recent development, akpom struck in the 91st minute to encourage O’Neil, but by then the game had been lost. Arsenal’s work, and indeed Dowman’s work, had been done.

"He's 16 years old, and we have to be cautious of that" 💫Mikel Arteta reacts to an incredible performance from Max Dowman as Arsenal put FOUR past Ipswich 🔴Don't miss the Carabao Cup on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/AIcAbMx6ub.

On managing the hype that surrounds Dowman, Arteta stated: “What we have to do is look after him. He’s 16 years old, you don’t see that in this league. In other leagues in Europe, that’s a totally different context, but in this league, with the demands... We need to make sure that every time we throw him in it’s in the right context with the right preparation.”.

Conor Coady shares his thoughts on Arteta’s role in Dowman’s development:.

"He'll know how to nurture him!" 🗣️Conor Coady says Mikel Arteta is the perfect manager for Max Dowman 👏 pic.twitter.com/YdgLxfKiOf.

Asked about Dowman’s two-goal performance, Arteta said: “A joy to have him, Marli [Salmon] as well. Seventeen years old, to play at that level with the physicality they have to be able to handle that level, it’s remarkable. Max, yeah, it’s inevitable to talk about him when he scores and he creates the moments he has created tonight. It’s normal.”.

In a recent development, he added: “He is coping better and better and better, he did the action where he regains the ball and wins it in the first goal, he loses his man... He’s an unbelievable player because of the character that he has and how much he loves to play on the biggest stage and still handles the situation with such naturality.”.

It has been revealed that speaking in his post-match press conference, Mikel Arteta remarked: “Really pleased with a lot of things we did tonight, the way we attacked the game, how dominant, fluid and aggressive we were, right from the beginning to try to influence the result. We scored two very early goals that gave us obviously a great platform for the game.

Industry observers note that “Individually some big performances as well. Some debuts tonight which is great to see as well, so we take a lot of positives from tonight.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sheffield Wednesday find themselves in a peculiar position regarding their academy, as a lot of young homegrown talents introduced themselves to the fanbase at Championship level last season due to "circumstances," but now need to find regular game time elsewhere.

That's the view of newly introduced Owls boss Dave Challinor, who has hinted that a few loan departures may be on the cards for some of the younger players in the squad who put themselves in the limelight during their difficult campaign last season under administration.

Wednesday's ability to build a squad over the past summer window has meant that, despite some fans looking forward to seeing these young players become the core of a newly introduced-look side, they've fallen by the wayside.

Challinor stated that Ernie Weaver, one of the early standouts from last season before being sidelined for the majority of the campaign with a foot injury, could be someone who leaves on a short-term deal in January, following the likes of Charlie McNeill, Cole McGhee and Reece Johnson, who all played some part in the Championship last season.

These five players should also be tipped for a loan move in the near future to get some valuable game time, too.

In a recent development, dave Challinor namedropped a couple of other players who could leave the club on loan at some point in the near future. One of those was fellow centre-back Gabriel Otegbayo.

According to recent reports, the Irish Under-21 international epitomised the chances that young players got last season while the club was in administration. The former Burnley academy man made 35 Championship appearances last season, including a run of 23 starts in the final 25 games.

Otegbayo began this season as one of the first-choice defenders under Henrik Pedersen, too, starting four of the first five in league action and scoring in his one appearance off the bench against Bromley in that 7-2 demolition.

Sources indicate that since that fifth game, though, the 21-year-old hasn't started in the league, and he's to feature in a matchday squad in League One under Challinor. Indeed, his only appearance under the upcoming boss came in the 4-0 EFL Trophy defeat against Accrington Stanley.

Wednesday fans weren't too enamoured with his performances in the early stages of the season, and also feel that he could benefit from a spell elsewhere.

The other player mentioned by Challinor as a potential loan option was midfielder Jarvis Thornton, who signed a newly introduced two-year deal with the Owls this past summer.

The 20-year-old has been at Wednesday since he was eight years old and was one of the many academy graduates who made their first-team debuts last season. He was one of the main features of their run to the EFL Cup third round, and he made 23 league appearances, too.

According to recent reports, this season, though, Thornton has been one of the main victims of the midfield being strengthened at Hillsborough. The returns of Barry Bannan and Jaiden Heskey, plus the addition of Billy Mitchell, have made it difficult for him to get minutes.

His last league appearance came in that 7-2 win over Bromley nearly three months ago, and he's made a matchday squad just once since then.

The new contract ensures that the decision-makers at Wednesday think he has a bright future, but he may need to begin to realise that elsewhere.

It was a proud moment for Sean Fusire against Accrington Stanley in the EFL Trophy, as he wore the captain's armband for the first time. Unfortunately, the Zimbabwe international hasn't been able to stake a claim for regular league minutes this season, though.

Sources indicate that the 21-year-old, unlike the others on this list so far, has actually spent time out on loan from Sheffield Wednesday. He spent the second half of the 2024/25 campaign at Carlisle United in League Two, but was then thrust into Championship action last year.

Only seven players played more league minutes than Fusire last season, but the full-back only has a couple in League One this year, coming on for the final stages of Henrik Pedersen's final game in charge at Doncaster Rovers.

Under Challinor, he has appearances in cup competitions, but hasn't made a league squad yet. You feel that, once the January window opens, he'll be one of the first out the door.

It has been revealed that it was a pleasant surprise for Wednesday fans to see George Brown starting against Accrington Stanley. It was the 20-year-old's first appearance in nearly 11 months after a season plagued by injury.

In a recent development, like Weaver, it was a real frustration to see him sidelined during the campaign in which he'd have gotten exposure at Championship level. He scored twice in just seven second-tier games last year, including one of their two wins all year at Portsmouth, and looked very promising.

He needs game time, but he won't get it at Hillsborough anytime soon. A good loan move away, perhaps at the top of the National League, could be massively beneficial to his chances of making it back in the senior fold in South Yorkshire.

Sources indicate that there arguably isn't a more exciting talent on Sheffield Wednesday's books right now than Will Grainger. The Welsh Under-19 international only just turned 18 earlier this month, and broke through towards the end of last season, scoring in a 4-1 defeat against Oxford United.

He also extended his contract with the Owls over the summer, but he, too, has been a victim of the strengthening of the squad, especially across the frontline.

In a recent development, do you think Will Grainger will be a major player in Sheffield Wednesday's bid to rise back up the EFL? Let us know in the comments.

Wednesday won't just be wanting to loan him out to any club for minutes; they'll be taking great care with this decision, as the 18-year-old could be a cornerstone of this upcoming era under the Arise ownership.

A good League Two move could work wonders for Grainger and put him in brilliant standing to properly break into the Owls' senior side next season, if they remain in League One.

Zohran Mamdani squared off with Upcoming York media and now the city's mayor will need a few months to recover.

As he revealed Friday while announcing plans to replace Rikers Island jail, Mamdani was playing in a soccer match against the local press corps at an indoor pitch in lower Manhattan when he tore his right Achilles tendon. Consequently, Mamdani is now using crutches and a walking boot, which he expects to be in for the next six to eight weeks.

'I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch and I forgot that I was 35,' Mamdani told gathered media on Friday at City Hall, where he was forced to rely on crutches.

Mamdani hopes to be back playing soccer again in nine months.

Sources indicate that local media may not be to blame here. As Mamdani told the Latest York Post, he arrived late to the game and began playing without properly stretching. What's more, the Post reported that Mamdani was overheard asking his police guards which reporter tackled him, only to be told he went down untouched.

Despite Mamdani's injury, team City Hall beat the local media, 8-4.

In a recent development, as he revealed Friday while announcing plans to close Rikers Island, Mamdani was playing  against the local press corps when tore his Achilles. Now he's in a boot (pictured).

Zohran Mamdani and wife Rama Duwaji are seen during a Brazil-Morocco World Cup match.

Industry observers note that born in Uganda and raised in Manhattan's Morningside Heights neighborhood, Mamdani played cricket and soccer in his youth. He even suited up for Bowdoin College's JV team during his days at the Maine school. Then later, as an adult, he became a shareholder of Spanish second-division club Real Oviedo.

But his biggest impact on the sport came over the summer, when New York welcomed thousands of tourists for the World Cup action at MetLife Stadium in nearby East Rutherford, New Jersey.

It has been revealed that upset with ticket prices for the matches, Mamdani organized more than 100 free watch parties around the city. The events were well attended and helped locals engage with the tournament even though no actual matches were played in New York.

Zohran Mamdani, center, joined by, from left, United States soccer star Tim Weah NYC World Cup Czar Maya Handa, and Fresh York council member Yusef Salaam back in May.

According to recent reports, 'We said from the beginning that the World Cup belongs to New Yorkers. This summer, we proved it,' Mamdani said in a statement. 'In the most international city on earth, you didn't need thousands of dollars to be part of the world's game.

'A kid in Corona, a nurse in Bay Ridge and a small business owner in Little Haiti could all celebrate together — for free or at a price they could afford,' he continued. 'That's what we mean when we talk about a city for the many.

Sources indicate that 'This summer, strangers became neighbors on Open Streets and in free Fan Fests across the city because government made room for people to come together. And long after the confetti is swept away, Newly introduced Yorkers will keep what we built: safer streets, faster buses, stronger protections, closer neighbors and the memory of a summer when the whole world felt at home here.'.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chris Sutton has said he can ‘only see one result’ from Liverpool’s showdown against Manchester United at Anfield on Sunday afternoon.

The home side go into the fixture 10 points and 14 places ahead of their arch-rivals, for whom this is a first game in charge for latest head coach Mauricio Pochettino.

The Reds’ home record in the Premier League so far this season has been poor, with just one win from five, but victory today would see them close to within one point of third-placed Manchester City.

In his weekly Premier League column for BBC Sport, Sutton voiced his belief that the visitors won’t have any ‘new manager bounce’ at Anfield and has forecast Liverpool to win handsomely.

The former Chelsea striker wrote: ‘Liverpool are still a work in progress, and United have picked up some results at Anfield recently – two draws and a win in their past three visits – but I can only see one result here, and it is a home victory.

‘Pochettino will probably look to defend and play on the counterattack, and they might get some chances that way, but Liverpool are going to win. The only question is how many they will score.

Industry observers note that ‘Carrick began by beating Manchester City and Arsenal in his first two games in January. Pochettino might start by being on the wrong end of a pummelling.’.

Sutton has predicted a resounding 4-0 win for Liverpool, matching the scoreline from this fixture in April 2022.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Sources indicate that considering the form and league positions of the teams, objectively the Reds ought to go into this game as clear favourites. When fifth plays host to second from bottom in the Premier League, the former would naturally be expected to win.

However, the pundit referenced Man United’s good record at Anfield since the famous 7-0 drubbing in March 2023, and Liverpool were also widely expected to win on a couple of those occasions.

Pochettino has never lost his first match at any of the five clubs he’s previously managed, and Reds fans might naturally be wary that the players who effectively downed tools under Michael Carrick will suddenly have a spring in their step today.

The good news for Iraola is that he has a mostly fully-fit squad, with Virgil van Dijk and Dominik Szoboszlai overcoming minor issues over the past couple of weeks and Ryan Gravenberch available once more, and there were no fresh injury casualties over the international window.

The Liverpool head coach has had a reasonably good start to his reign but is still waiting on a genuine ‘statement’ victory. That would change if Sutton’s emphatic prediction comes to light, but we’re sure that every Kopite would gladly take a win by any means against our biggest rivals.

  • Birmingham's strong start to the Championship season followed an intriguing summer transfer window, but they were swiftly knocked off the division's summit last weekend after a lacklustre defeat to fellow promotion hopefuls, Stoke City, on Saturday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Birmingham City's recent progress has led to a strong amount of player turnover at St. Andrew's @ Knighthead Park, and now there is a strong focus on what could be in store come the opening of the January transfer window.

It has been made no secret that Chris Davies' side are looking to reach the Premier League in the near future, with the 41-year-old receiving plenty of backing from Knighthead Capital Management during a near two-and-a-half-year tenure.

Birmingham's strong start to the Championship season followed an intriguing summer transfer window, but they were swiftly knocked off the division's summit last weekend after a lacklustre defeat to fellow promotion hopefuls, Stoke City, on Saturday.

Sources indicate that it was an encounter in which plenty of concerns which came to a head last season for Blues were evident, including a lack of urgency in attacking areas. As such, the debate has continued as to which areas need strengthening within Davies' squad with the January window looming large.

On top of such decisions, it feels inevitable that some of those within the Blues ranks may move on to new pastures, including rather luckless full-back, Lee Buchanan.

Buchanan's senior career began seven years ago, earning a first-team berth with Derby County under Phillip Cocu for the 2019/20 campaign.

It wasn't until the 2020/21 campaign, which saw the Rams narrowly escape relegation under the management of Wayne Rooney, where the full-back earned his major breakthrough with 37 appearances, being named the club's Young Player of the Season in the process.

During the early weeks of that particular season, Buchanan was called up to the England Under-20s squad, where he revealed that Rooney, who became his Birmingham boss just under three years later, predicted a bright future in the game for the defender.

“He’s England’s all-time top scorer so speaking to him obviously helps a lot," said Buchanan.

“He told me to go out there and enjoy myself, to keep doing what I do for the club and that he’s sure I’d be fine.".

The 2021/22 season was a difficult campaign for Derby, although Buchanan was one of several academy graduates to emerge with credit for his performance levels at Pride Park which would have resulted in Championship survival, were it not for a 21-point deduction.

The defender was then the subject of a controversial departure to Bundesliga side, Werder Bremen, where he would link up with current Birmingham teammate, Marvin Ducksch, for the first time, making 21 appearances in the German top-flight before swiftly returning to the Midlands under current Rams head coach, John Eustace.

At 22 years of age, Blues certainly invested in Buchanan's potential in their first transfer window of the Knighthead era, with the left-back penning a five-year deal.

Three of those have now passed, and the defender's time in B9 has become one to forget, not least due to an unfortunate ACL injury which kept him sidelined between December 2024 and August 2026.

Buchanan has only played 40 times for Birmingham since his arrival in July 2023, with the bulk of stated appearances coming during the club's relegation campaign of 2023/24, prior to Alex Cochrane's arrival.

Davies opted to select Buchanan during pre-season and in the 1-0 win over Swansea City in the EFL Cup first round following his recovery with the Blues boss saying: “I looked at him before the game and thought if he’s called upon he's ready to go now and it claims a lot for the man, as well as the player.”.

Recent findings suggest that whilst Buchanan's character has never been doubted, his long-term position at St. Andrew's is far from secure, and that was certainly the case in the summer window.

In January, Davies was in no rush to loan out the defender despite Kai Wagner arriving as back-up to Cochrane, and even though the German swiftly returned to Philadelphia Union, Buchanan also attracted transfer interest.

League One promotion hopefuls, Luton Town and Reading, were credited with interest, but, ultimately, a move failed to materialise.

At 25 years of age, Buchanan is set to be entering the prime of his career, and the chances of reigniting his career seem very little at Birmingham right now.

Cochrane has continued as Davies' mainstay following the exit of Wagner, and whilst Kristoffer Lund has also suffered injury misfortune this season, the seven-time USMNT international does appear to be ahead of Buchanan in the pecking order.

In a recent development, blues fans, could Lee Buchanan have become a key figure at St. Andrew's without his injury woes? Comment below!

In January, there will be 18 months left on the full-back's contract, making it a prime opportunity for Blues to recoup some form of cash on his services, whilst allowing the player to rediscover form and match sharpness after just one competitive appearance 23 months.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Where you are can matter as much as who you are.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Where you are can matter as much as who you are. Banks, power grids and satellite-navigation systems all depend on knowing where a request or a signal comes from, yet claims about location are notoriously easy to fake. Spoofing and jamming attacks on satellite navigation, for example, are on the rise. Writing in Nature, Kavuri et al.1 report an experiment in which the position of a distant party is certified using the peculiar correlations between quantum particles, known as entanglement. Remarkably, the scheme’s security does not rely on trust of any quantum hardware, only on measurement statistics and the fact that nothing travels faster than light.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stoke City could have the chance to go to the top of the Championship on Wednesday night, depending on how results on Tuesday go, when they host Millwall and former boss Alex Neil at the bet365 Stadium.

Stoke have continued their scintillating run of form under Mark Robins with a 1-0 home victory over Birmingham City at the weekend, leapfrogging the Blues in the Championship table, and now sit only behind Middlesbrough on goal difference as things stand.

Depending on how Boro get on against Swansea City on Tuesday night, Stoke could go to the top of the league with another three points in this fixture, though returning boss Neil is bound to make it as difficult as possible for the Potters.

Millwall haven't been at their best as of late, with just one win in their last seven league games, but with just two defeats in their last 16 games against Stoke, they have more often than not had the upper hand in this encounter in recent memory.

For Stoke, Djibril Soumare and George Hirst picked up minor knocks against Birmingham and will need to be assessed; Ethan Galbraith could come back into the side after illness, whilst Millwall wait on decisions on Luke Cundle, Josh Coburn, and Romain Esse, as Football League World takes a look at each player set to miss Wednesday's clash in the Potteries.

French striker Lamine Cisse has shown sparks of his talent this campaign, particularly in the games against Bolton Wanderers and Watford, but has been out of action since being forced off in Stoke's goalless draw with Bristol City a month ago.

It has since been confirmed that the 23-year-old will likely be out of action until Christmas, providing George Hirst, Robert Bozenik, and Sam Gallagher with chances to impress Robins up top.

Veteran full-back Aaron Cresswell has yet to make an appearance this season after extending his stay in North Staffordshire for another year over the summer, having picked up an injury during pre-season.

Robins confirmed that the 36-year-old was back on the grass training last month, but he still remains some way short of fitness, and isn't expected to make a return to the pitch just yet.

Luca Bombino has found minutes at left wing-back recently following an injury to Eric Bocat and impressed, with the American looking to make his mark in the Championship following his potential $5 million (£3.7 million) move from MLS side San Diego late in the summer window.

After picking up a yellow card in the first half against Birmingham, Bombino mistimed his challenge around the hour mark on Patrick Roberts, receiving his marching orders, and as a result, will be suspended for this game, as Bocat or Justin Devenny will likely take his place on the left flank for the Potters against Millwall.

Ato Ampah has endured a torrid time with injuries ever since joining Stoke from Chelsea's academy for a potential £3 million in January 2026, with the young winger still yet to make a senior appearance for the Potters nearly a year later.

The England youth international was on the cusp of a first-team return in October before a further injury setback means he will have to wait even longer for his Potters debut, as the youngster will be praying 2027 is his year.

Onto Millwall now, as left-back Zak Sturge is set to miss the trip to North Staffordshire after receiving an early red card in his side's narrow 1-0 home defeat to Queens Park Rangers at the weekend.

This means Alfie Doughty could come back into the fold to face his former side on Wednesday, or Jordi Osei-Tutu could be preferred in that role.

Mathis Servais joined Millwall in the summer from Belgian outfit KV Mechelen to much excitement, but with just nine minutes of Championship football to shout about nearly six months later, it hasn't exactly been the dream start to life at The Den he would've hoped for.

A hamstring injury in pre-season forced him to wait to make his debut, and another injury sustained in the following international break has kept him out of action since, and it doesn't look like he will be ready for this one.

Arguably the biggest absence for Millwall is French defender Tristan Crama, who, after an incredible full debut year for the Lions, has struggled with injury woes this campaign.

The 25-year-old has been limited to just five appearances so far this season, injuring both of his ankles, and has been absent from the side since Halloween's 4-1 victory over Derby County, where he was forced to come off just after the hour mark.

Filip Marschall joined Millwall in the summer from League One Stevenage to provide an alternative option between the sticks to Lukas Jensen and Max Crocombe, but after four appearances, he suffered ankle ligament damage against Lincoln City.

Jensen has since returned to the side and is expected to start between the sticks as the former Aston Villa youth player recovers.

Who do you think will be the biggest miss from this fixture, and what are your score predictions? Share your thoughts below!

Ryan Leonard, like Crama, has been missing from Millwall's squad since the 4-1 home victory over Derby, and Neil issued an enhancement on the 34-year-old in early November.

Sources indicate that neil noted: "About eight days ago, Ryan Leonard contacted his knee on the left-hand side at our place. It’s been sore since, but it’s getting to the stage where the pain’s not dying down. We got it scanned, and unfortunately, Lenny’s got an concern just above his knee. He won’t be back within the next month.".

Is Mauricio Pochettino’s job at Manchester United the toughest in the Premier League?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manchester United hired Mauricio Pochettino as their next manager to replace Michael Carrick, who managed just one win in 10 games.
  • His appointment makes him Manchester United’s eighth permanent manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.
  • According to recent reports, pochettino brings considerable Premier League experience after previous spells with Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United hired Mauricio Pochettino as their next manager to replace Michael Carrick, who managed just one win in 10 games.

His appointment makes him Manchester United’s eighth permanent manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

According to recent reports, pochettino brings considerable Premier League experience after previous spells with Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea. He has also managed Paris Saint-Germain before the USA job.

As he faces Liverpool for his first game on Sunday, the question arises: is he facing the toughest job in the Premier League?

The question was posed on BBC Radio about who is going to have more pressure, Pochettino or Thomas Frank at Crystal Palace.

According to former Premier League defender Nedum Onuoha, the expectations surrounding Manchester United will make the Argentine’s job considerably harder.

According to recent reports, pochettino is preparing for his first game in charge of Manchester United, with Liverpool waiting at Anfield on November 22. However, the challenge facing the latest manager goes beyond getting results on the pitch.

Onuoha believes Pochettino will have to deal with constant discussion and criticism about his work, much of it coming from former United players who are now in the media.

Choosing between Pochettino and Frank, Onuoha noted, “Probably Pochettino, because every former Manchester United player works in the media, so there will always be discussion around what he is doing.

“Whereas Frank can just enjoy playing his football at Crystal Palace. If he does well then it is great, if he doesn’t do well then it is still OK.

“But from Pochettino’s perspective, if Manchester United finish the season 15th in the Premier League, whether we like it or not, there will be some criticism of him because he’s had 28 games to do something.”.

The comments just highlight the difference in expectations at the two clubs. Frank may have more freedom to work without the same level of attention, while Pochettino will be judged from day one against the standards historically associated with Manchester United. That is one substantial problem for Pochettino.

According to recent reports, rory Smith from The Observer highlighted another glaring problem at United. Highlighting a major problem, Smith stated, “there is a cycle element to Manchester United whereby a manager comes in, makes things a bit better, and then within a year to 18 months they aren’t challenging for titles again because the Premier League has changed since they were a dominant force.”.

Pochettino’s first taste of action as a United manager will be against Liverpool at Anfield on November 22. That opening fixture will give him an immediate test, but the bigger task will be to get back United to winning ways, step by step.

Will the Manchester United job be without pressure for Mauricio Pochettino? Absolutely Not.

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.
